class Attribute#
#include <attribute.h>

The base interface for all continuous material and property attributes.

This class defines the common interface for sampling an attribute map, including material volume fractions and values like density or elastic modulus.

Subclassed by CoordinateReframedAttribute, FloatAttribute, Vec3Attribute, Vec4Attribute, VolumeFractionsAttribute

enumerator vec4#

A glm::vec4.

enumerator vfm_ptr#

A VolumeFractionMapPtr.

struct AttributeSampleContext#
#include <attribute.h>

Optional CellMap location information shared by one attribute sample.

position is always expressed in the current consuming node’s coordinates. This context does not retain a root-world coordinate system; it only avoids repeating CellMap inversion while sampling lattice-specific coordinate adapters. Mapped lattice leaves may also supply compact source-component provenance.

class AttributeSet#
#include <attribute_set.h>

A container for multiple Attributes assigned to a Node.

This class acts as a key-value store mapping attribute names to their evaluating Attribute objects. It handles the sampling of all contained attributes at a specific point.

class FloatAttribute : public Attribute#
#include <float_attribute.h>

A scalar attribute defined by an expression, native function, constant or float volume.

The source is set once, by a constructor or by one of the setters. The setters are one-shot: set_expression(), set_function() and set_value() throw std::runtime_error if any source (expression, function, constant or volume) is already set. A default-constructed attribute has no source until a setter is called. Subclasses such as DerivedFloatAttribute and NoiseFloatAttribute override sample() and the bound queries.

Subclassed by CellMapGuardedAttribute, ComponentScalarAttribute, CoordinateFieldAttribute, CurvatureAttribute, DerivedFloatAttribute, DistanceFieldAttribute, NoiseFloatAttribute, ScatteredFloatAttribute

Public Types

A function for spatial grading.

The function takes the spatial coordinates (x, y, z) and the signed distance to the surface and returns a floating point value for some attribute.

virtual std::optional<std::pair<double, double>> value_bounds() const#

Returns the range of values this field is known to stay in, or std::nullopt.

Known by construction, never estimated by sampling. A constant knows its value; fields that know their range (noise, clamp(), ease(), transfer(), …) override this. ScalarParameter adopts it, so such a field can size an operator’s bounding box.

Returns:

The (minimum, maximum) pair, or std::nullopt when the range is unknown.

class Vec3Attribute : public Attribute#
#include <vec3_attribute.h>

An attribute that stores a function for spatial grading that returns a vec3.

This class can be used to create any spatially varying 3-component attribute. When used for representing color, the vec3 values should be in the range [0, 1].

Subclassed by CellMapCoordinateAttribute, CellMapJacobianAttribute, CellMapWorldDirectionAttribute, ComponentDirectionAttribute, DerivedVec3Attribute, NoiseVec3Attribute, NormalFieldAttribute, ScatteredVec3Attribute

class ScalarParameter#
#include <scalar_parameter.h>

A geometry parameter that is either a constant or a spatially varying scalar field.

Operators whose parameters may vary in space (offset distance, shell thickness, blend radius, tube radius, twist rate) store one of these instead of a double. A constant takes a fast path with no virtual call. A field is any FloatAttribute, sampled with value(x, y, z, d). A FloatAttribute built from a double is detected and treated as a constant.

Optional hints describe a field where they are known:

  • bounds(): the smallest and largest value the field takes, used to size bounding boxes. Constants always know their bounds.

  • lipschitz(): an upper bound L on the field’s slope, |t(p) - t(q)| <= L |p - q|. An operator that subtracts the field from a distance (f - t) can divide by 1 + L to keep a safe distance bound. Constants have L = 0. A field that knows its range or slope by construction (FloatAttribute::value_bounds() and lipschitz_bound(), for example noise, clamp() or ease()) supplies them itself; the caller’s with_bounds() and with_lipschitz() override them. Nothing is estimated by sampling.

The value is copyable and cheap to copy; copies share the field. Nodes call clone() in their own clone() so each evaluation thread gets its own field, the same way they clone FloatAttribute members today.

class VolumeFractionsAttribute : public Attribute#
#include <volume_fractions_attribute.h>

An attribute that stores a set of volume fraction (functions) for different materials.

The attribute contains a spatially graded function for each material. The attribute can be sampled at a point to get the volume fractions for each material. The attribute can be used to create a material distribution for a point in space. Sampled fractions are returned exactly as the functions evaluate; they are not clamped or normalized to sum to 1. Each material may be added only once.

Note

Functions in this class can be defined as math expressions or as native (lambda) functions.

Note

If using the math expression strings, you can use the following variables in the expression to spatially grade: x, y, z, rho, phic, r, theta, phis, d (signed distance) For more documentation on the math expression syntax, see the Exprtk documentation: ArashPartow/exprtk

class DerivedFloatAttribute : public FloatAttribute#
#include <derived_attribute.h>

An immutable scalar attribute computed from other typed attributes.

Dependencies form an immutable graph and are sampled in the same consumer-relative coordinates as this attribute: in double precision through sample(x, y, z, d), and with the caller’s context through sample(context). clone() recursively clones the full dependency graph. map_range accepts input bounds in either order (they must differ) and extrapolates linearly. fallback returns its single parameter wherever the dependency throws or produces a non-finite value, for example outside a CellMap domain.

Shaping operations:

  • ease: parameters {easing, shape}. The input is clamped to [0, 1] and passed through an Easing curve (see easing.h), so the result stays in [0, 1].

  • transfer: parameters {interpolation, x0, y0, x1, y1, …}, interpolation 0 for linear and 1 for smooth. A PiecewiseCurve through the control points; it holds the end values beyond them.

Geometry operations:

  • vector_angle: two Vec3 inputs, parameter {degrees}: the angle between them, in degrees (1) or radians (0). 90 degrees where either vector is zero.

  • inverse_distance_weight: N scalar distance inputs, parameters {index, exponent p}: the normalized inverse-distance weight d_i^-p / sum_j d_j^-p of input index, in [0, 1]. Distances are clamped at 0 (inside a body counts as on it); where some are 0, those inputs share the weight equally. With two body distances and index 1 this is the two-body field, 0 at the first body and 1 at the second; with point distances it is inverse-distance (Shepard) weighting.

value_bounds() and lipschitz_bound() carry the inputs’ known range and slope through the operations that allow it (sums, products, clamp, normalize, map_range, ease, transfer, …).

class CellMapGuardedAttribute : public FloatAttribute#
#include <cell_map_guarded_attribute.h>

A scalar attribute defined everywhere: a fallback outside a CellMap’s active domain.

Each sample first locates the point in the CellMap. Outside the active domain the fallback is returned without evaluating the wrapped attribute; inside, the wrapped attribute is sampled with the located CellMap context, so CellMap coordinate adapters (logical position, cell index, phase) reuse the location instead of inverting the map again. Any other failure or a non-finite value also returns the fallback. This avoids the exception that CellMap adapters raise outside the domain, which matters when a field-driven Mix samples its weight over a whole bounding box.

class CoordinateSource#
#include <coordinate_field_attribute.h>

Something that assigns named coordinates to points of space.

Curves, the curve-based nodes (Tube, Extrude, Revolve, Sweep) and the deformation maps of Warp (WarpMap) describe space in their own coordinates: position along a curve, angle around it, position in a profile, where a point pulls back to under a warp. A CoordinateSource evaluates those coordinates at any point, so CoordinateFieldAttribute can turn each one into a field for grading material or driving other geometry.

Thread safety: coordinate() may keep per-call state in fields it samples, so every thread uses its own clone(). Sources share immutable geometry between clones and deep-clone any ScalarParameter fields.

Subclassed by CurveCoordinates, ExtrudeGeometry, LoftGeometry, RevolveGeometry, SweepGeometry, TubeGeometry, WarpMap

std::shared_ptr<FloatAttribute> two_body_field(const std::shared_ptr<Node> &first, const std::shared_ptr<Node> &second, double exponent = 1.0, double voxel_size = 0.5, double bandwidth = 10.0)#

Returns a field that is 0 at the first body, 1 at the second, and grades smoothly between them.

The value is d1^p / (d1^p + d2^p), with d1 and d2 the distances to the two bodies (0 inside), built from two DistanceFieldAttributes and DerivedFloatAttribute’s inverse_distance_weight. p = 1 gives an even grade; larger p keeps values near 0 and 1 longer and makes the switch sharper midway. The range is [0, 1]. Choose a bandwidth at least as large as the gap between the bodies, so both distances are accurate where the field grades (see DistanceFieldAttribute).

Parameters:

  • first – The body where the field is 0.

  • second – The body where the field is 1.

  • exponent – The power p, positive.

  • voxel_size – Voxel size in mm used to prepare the bodies.

  • bandwidth – Distance in mm around each body’s box where its distance is evaluated.

class DistanceFieldAttribute : public FloatAttribute#
#include <distance_field_attribute.h>

A scalar attribute whose value is the distance to another body (a node), evaluated natively so it can drive grading through map_range(), clamp(), and other modifiers.

The body is any OpenVCAD node: a primitive, a Mesh, a CAD part, a boolean tree, or a mapped structure. The constructor clones the body and prepares the clone with the given voxel size and bandwidth, so the caller’s node is never modified. Each sample evaluates the prepared body’s signed distance at the sample position (the consuming node’s coordinates), negative inside the body. With signed_distance false the absolute value is returned, which measures distance to the body’s surface from either side.

Range: the value is as accurate as the body’s own field within its prepared bounding box expanded by the bandwidth (exact for analytic primitives, voxel-accurate for mesh SDFs, which also clamp to the bandwidth). Beyond that region the body has no value, and the attribute returns the distance to the expanded box plus the bandwidth, a lower bound that keeps grading monotone far away. Choose a bandwidth at least as large as the distances the grading uses (for example the liner thickness).

Thread safety: clone() clones the prepared body, so every cloned tree evaluates its own body copy. Units are millimetres.

class NoiseFloatAttribute : public FloatAttribute#
#include <noise_attribute.h>

A scalar noise field: simplex (gradient) noise or cellular (Worley) distances, with fractal octaves.

The value depends only on the point and the NoiseSettings (see noise.h), so the same seed gives the same field on every platform and in every thread. Sampling keeps no state.

Range: simplex noise is in [-1, 1]; cellular F1 is in [0, sqrt(3)] and F2 and F2 - F1 in [0, 2 sqrt(3)], in cell units (typical values stay below about 1.2). value_bounds() reports these and lipschitz_bound() an analytic slope bound per mm, so the field can drive geometry (an offset, a shell thickness) without extra hints. Units: frequency is in features per mm.

Returns the angle in degrees (or radians) between a body’s surface normal and a direction.

0 where the surface faces the direction, 90 where it is parallel to it, 180 where it faces away. For example, with the build direction +Z, downward-facing overhangs read near 180. class NormalFieldAttribute : public Vec3Attribute#
#include <normal_field_attribute.h>

A vector field: the unit surface normal of another body (a node), extended through space.

The value is the normalized gradient of the body’s signed distance, by central differences of a DistanceFieldAttribute this attribute owns (so the body is cloned and prepared once, exactly as for a distance field, and the caller’s node is never modified). The step is half the voxel size.

On the surface it is the outward normal. Off the surface it is the gradient at the point, which for an exact signed distance is the normal at the closest surface point, so the field is constant along each normal line. Where the gradient vanishes (on a medial axis, for example a sphere’s centre) it is the zero vector. Beyond the distance field’s band it follows the band’s lower-bound fallback, which points away from the body’s bounding box.

Use it to grade by orientation (dot or angle with a direction, see DerivedFloatAttribute::Operation::vector_angle) or to move material along normals. Thread safety: clone() clones the prepared body, as DistanceFieldAttribute does.

class CurvatureAttribute : public FloatAttribute#
#include <curvature_attribute.h>

A scalar field: the curvature of another body’s surface (a node), in 1/mm.

The value comes from the gradient g and Hessian H of the body’s signed distance, taken by central differences (19 samples) of a DistanceFieldAttribute this attribute owns. The body is cloned and prepared once, as for a distance field; the caller’s node is not modified. The step is half the voxel size. On the surface it is the surface’s curvature; off the surface it is the curvature of the level set through the point (for an exact distance, that of the offset surface).

Kinds:

  • mean: (|g|^2 tr H - g^T H g) / (2 |g|^3), the average of the principal curvatures. Positive on convex skin (1/R on a sphere of radius R), negative in hollows, 0 on planes and saddles balanced between the two.

  • gaussian: g^T adj(H) g / |g|^4, the product of the principal curvatures (1/R^2 on a sphere, 0 on cylinders and planes, negative on saddles).

  • maximum: the largest absolute principal curvature, 1 / (tightest bend radius). Tight bends and sharp edges read high; a sharp edge reads about 1 / step, so it marks where a fillet may be needed.

Where the gradient vanishes (a medial point) the value is 0. Accuracy: second-order in the step on smooth surfaces; features smaller than the step are smoothed over. Thread safety: clone() clones the prepared body, as DistanceFieldAttribute does.

class ScatteredFloatAttribute : public FloatAttribute#
#include <scattered_attribute.h>

A scalar field from values known at scattered points (measurements, simulation nodes, sensors).

Evaluates a shared, immutable ScatteredInterpolator (see it for the methods, their cost and their behaviour away from the data). clone() shares the interpolator, and sampling uses per-thread buffers, so clones evaluate in parallel. The field is defined everywhere, not only near the points. value_bounds() reports the data range for nearest and inverse-distance interpolation, which never leave it; radial-basis fits may overshoot and report none.

class LookupTableConverter : public AttributeConverterBase#
#include <lookup_table_converter.h>

A generic lookup-table-based attribute converter.

This converter maps one or more input attribute values to one or more output attribute values using a lookup table. It supports two interpolation modes:

  • STEP: Range-based matching where the input value falls within [low, high] of each entry. First match wins. Output can be any Attribute::Value type (double, vec3, vec4, etc.).

  • LINEAR: Sorted-point interpolation where the input must be a double and the output values are interpolated/clamped between neighboring entries. Supported output types are double, vec3, vec4, and volume-fraction maps. LINEAR mode needs exactly one output attribute. With one input, entries are sorted by input_low. With two inputs, each entry’s input_points gives a grid point, the entries must form a complete rectilinear grid, and the output is bilinearly interpolated (clamped at the grid edges).

Inputs must be scalar (double) samples. In single-input STEP and in LINEAR mode, a missing input passes the samples through unchanged, as does a STEP input that matches no entry. Input samples are kept.

Multi-input STEP mode: When multiple input attributes are given, each entry must provide per-input ranges via input_ranges and one output value per input. Each input is matched independently against its own range (first match wins), and missing inputs are skipped. The matched output values are then written:

  • N inputs, several outputs: each matched input sets its own output attribute (outputs beyond N are ignored); unmatched inputs set nothing.

  • N inputs, 1 output: all-or-nothing. The output is written only when every input matched. The values are assembled: vec3 + double (in either order) becomes a vec4 with the double as alpha; any other combination writes the first input’s value.

struct LookupTableEntry#
#include <lookup_table_converter.h>

A single entry in a lookup table.

Which fields are read depends on the converter’s mode and input count:

  • Single-input STEP: [input_low, input_high] is the matching window, and output_values holds one value per output attribute.

  • Multi-input STEP: input_ranges holds one [low, high] pair per input attribute, and output_values holds one value per input attribute.

  • Single-input LINEAR: input_low is the interpolation knot, and output_values[0] is the value at that knot.

  • Two-input LINEAR: input_points holds the (input 0, input 1) grid point, and output_values holds exactly one value.

The point and range constructors also set input_low and input_high from the first point or range.

Public Functions

  • value – The output value at the knot.

Single-output convenience constructor for two-input LINEAR mode.

  • value – The output value at the grid point.

Each input is matched independently and produces its corresponding output value.

  • values – Output values, one per input attribute.

class ExpressionConverter : public AttributeConverterBase#
#include <expression_converter.h>

An attribute converter that evaluates mathematical expressions.

Uses ExpressionEvaluator (exprtk) to compute output attributes from input attributes via user-defined math strings.

Input attribute names are used directly as variable names in the expression string. For example, if input_attributes = {“temperature”}, then the expression “20 * temperature + 100” will read the “temperature” attribute sample and compute the result.

Each output attribute has its own expression string.

Inputs must be scalar (double) samples. If any input is missing at a point, the samples pass through unchanged. Otherwise each output is added or replaced and the input samples are kept. Expressions are compiled on the first convert() call, so a bad expression throws there.

Note

This converter is stateful (owns mutable ExpressionEvaluator instances). The clone() method produces a fresh instance for thread safety.

class VolumeFractionsExpressionConverter : public AttributeConverterBase#
#include <volume_fractions_expression_converter.h>

Converts scalar input attributes into volume fractions with math expressions.

Each expression evaluates to one material’s volume fraction. Input attribute names are available as variables inside every expression, and the converter writes the resulting material map to DefaultAttributes::VOLUME_FRACTIONS.

Inputs must be scalar (double) samples. If any input is missing at a point, the samples pass through unchanged. The fractions are written exactly as the expressions evaluate: they are not clamped or normalized to sum to 1. Expressions are compiled on the first convert() call.

Note

This converter is stateful because it owns compiled expression evaluators. clone() returns a fresh converter for thread-safe use.

Conflict resolvers#

Strategies that combine one attribute where several children of a node overlap.

class AttributeConflictResolver#
#include <attribute_conflict_resolver.h>

Combines the values of one attribute where several children of a node overlap.

A composition node (e.g. Union) uses a resolver when more than one child defines the same attribute at a sample point. All values passed to resolve() share the attribute’s return type.

Subclassed by AverageConflictResolver, CustomFloatConflictResolver, CustomVec4ConflictResolver, MaxConflictResolver, MinConflictResolver, SumConflictResolver

Public Functions

Combine overlapping attribute values into one.

Parameters:

values – The values from each overlapping child, all of the same type. Must not be empty.

Returns:

The combined value, of the same type as the inputs.

class MaxConflictResolver : public AttributeConflictResolver#
#include <builtins.h>

Resolves overlaps with the maximum value.

Scalars take the maximum. Vec3/Vec4 values follow the Vec4Mode. Volume-fraction maps are first averaged, then only the material(s) with the largest averaged fraction (within 1e-6) are kept and renormalized to sum to 1.
